packets.key_finding: Across three experiments including a representative five-country European sample (n=4207), default nudges shift risk-taking with medium-to-large effect sizes, but implementing a default (or having it refused) lowers ratings of the advisor's honesty and advice quality, and how the default is framed and presented also shifts the chosen allocation.
packets.methodology: Three behavioral experiments, one large representative multi-country European sample, on default framing in investment/wealth-management decisions.
packets.why_it_matters: Gives EU consumer-context evidence that defaults can anchor the chosen level (relevant to the preset-multiplier decision) while also measurably damaging perceived trust when a default is imposed or refused \u2014 the exact 'dark pattern' reputational risk the brief flags.
limitations: wealth-management advice context, not a round-up savings app
risk-taking allocation rather than a savings-amount outcome
no medium/long-term persistence data
packets.relevance_reason: EU-based experimental evidence on default framing effects on chosen level and on perceived manipulation, directly speaking to the brief's dark-pattern concern.
packets.title: Framing the Default Option Right
packets.abstract: ABSTRACT Defaults are powerful nudges to shape individuals' behavior: In three experiments, including a large experiment using representative samples from five European countries (n = 4207), we show that they can significantly affect risk‐taking by medium to large effect sizes. We also show that implementing a default nudge leads to a lower rating of the advice delivered by the wealth manager compared to no default, an effect that has a medium to large effect size. In addition, defaults the targeted individuals refuse result in lower advice ratings. These side effects call for caution before applying nudges and individualized defaults rather than a one‐size‐fits‐all approach. Additionally, we find evidence pointing to two small effects of framing in default presentation. First, asking how much individuals want to invest in the risky asset emphasizes risk. It reduces investment in the risky asset compared to asking them how much they want to leave on the safe account, particularly for more risk‐averse individuals. Second, asking individuals if they want to change a default allocation of 100% in the risky asset leads to more investment in the risky asset than asking them whether they accept such an allocation. Perceived wealth manager honesty appears to mediate the relationship between the default nudge and the rating of the advice.

packets.key_finding: After the EU Digital Markets Act mandated active-choice browser screens replacing preset defaults, Firefox usage rose 113% on iOS and 12% on Android relative to a no-mandate counterfactual, with effects persisting 15+ months after rollout.
packets.methodology: Difference-in-differences design exploiting the staggered rollout of EU DMA-mandated choice screens on iOS and Android.
packets.why_it_matters: The clearest large-scale, long-horizon evidence that a regulator-mandated active-choice screen can substantially and durably shift outcomes away from a preset default in a digital consumer product, directly informing whether active choice would meaningfully move enrolment relative to opt-in/opt-out and whether the effect fades.
limitations: Browser choice, not a financial savings product
Measures usage share, not amount saved or engagement depth
packets.relevance_reason: The strongest available evidence on active choice versus default persistence at scale in an EU-regulated consumer digital product, directly bearing on the entry-design decision.
packets.title: The Effect of Choice Screens on Mobile Browser Usage: Evidence from the EU Digital Markets Act
packets.abstract: Can active choice mitigate the effects of preset defaults? We study this question using a difference-in-differences design around the rollout of the EU’s Digital Markets Act, which required iOS and Android to display browser choice screens under certain conditions. We find large effects, with notable differences across platforms: from 15 months after the mandate onward, Firefox usage was 113 percent higher on iOS and 12 percent higher on Android relative to a no-mandate counterfactual. This gap is consistent with rollout differences, as Android showed choice screens primarily on new devices, whereas iOS also showed them on existing devices.Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.
packets.tldr: Large effects are found around the rollout of the EU’s Digital Markets Act, which required iOS and Android to display browser choice screens under certain conditions, with notable differences across platforms.

packets.key_finding: Across nine 401(k) plans, steady-state saving rates rise only 0.6% of income from automatic enrollment and 0.3% from default auto-escalation once job turnover, pre-vesting withdrawals, and opt-outs from escalation are accounted for; only 40% of those defaulted into auto-escalation actually escalate on the first date.
packets.methodology: Longitudinal administrative analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporating turnover, withdrawal, and opt-out dynamics.
packets.why_it_matters: The clearest quantified statement of the support team's objection: naive enrollment-lift numbers substantially overstate the real, medium-run increase in money saved once attrition and opt-out are accounted for.
limitations: retirement plans, not liquid consumer savings
employer-mediated context the brief says doesn't transfer
no direct measure of engagement or complaints
packets.relevance_reason: Directly contradicts the premise that default enrollment reliably translates into materially more saving, with quantified effect sizes.
packets.title: Smaller than We Thought? The Effect of Automatic Savings Policies
packets.abstract: Medium-and long-run dynamics undermine the effect of automatic enrollment and default savingsrate auto-escalation on retirement savings.Our analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporates the facts that employees frequently leave firms (often before matching contributions from their employer have fully vested), a large percentage of 401(k) balances are withdrawn upon employment separation, and many employees opt out of auto-escalation.Steady-state saving rates increase by 0.6% of income due to automatic enrollment and 0.3% of income due to default autoescalation.Only 40% of those with an auto-escalation default escalate on their first escalation date, and more opt out later.

packets.key_finding: A field experiment that made an autopay-minimum default less convenient reduced minimum-only payers by 23% after six months but did not significantly reduce credit card debt, because nudged cardholders mostly chose autopay amounts only slightly above the minimum and some stopped using autopay at all, increasing missed payments.
packets.methodology: Field experiment with card issuer, six-month follow-up on payment behavior and debt outcomes.
packets.why_it_matters: This is the closest real-world proof that a choice-architecture change can move a nominal enrollment/behavior metric while leaving the underlying outcome (debt, and by analogy, saved amount) unchanged or worse \u2014 exactly the 'vanity enrollment' risk our support team is warning about, in an actual consumer banking product rather than a pension.
limitations: studies debt repayment nudges, not savings sign-up
US credit card population, not EU app users
the specific nudge (shrouding) differs from opt-in/opt-out/active choice framing
packets.relevance_reason: Directly tests whether a choice-architecture nudge that changes headline behavior also changes the substantive financial outcome, in a genuine consumer financial product.
packets.title: The Semblance of Success in Nudging Consumers to Pay Down Credit Card Debt
packets.abstract: We test a nudge in a field experiment on credit cards. The nudge shrouds the autopay enrollment option for cardholders to automatically pay exactly the credit card minimum payment each month. After six months, the nudge decreases the fraction of cardholders who only pay exactly the minimum by 23 percent. However, the nudge does not significantly reduce credit card debt. Nudged cardholders often choose autopay amounts that are only slightly higher than the minimum payment. The nudge reduces autopay enrollment, which increases missed payments. The nudge reduces manual payments by autopay enrollees. Cardholders frequently lacking liquid cash best explains our results. (JEL C93, D12, D91, G21, G51)

packets.key_finding: Proposes a taxonomy and conceptual framework for when and how defaults produce downstream effects on consumer behavior over time, identifying time course, antecedent preferences, and trade-off salience as key moderators, and sets a research agenda to reconcile inconsistent findings.
packets.methodology: Conceptual/theoretical review synthesizing the consumer-default literature; no new empirical data. Abstract-only.
packets.why_it_matters: This is the review the brief asks for on the persistence question: it gives the conceptual machinery for predicting when a default's effect on enrollment will or won't persist into actual saved amounts, directly informing what to measure at 6-12 months and why heterogeneity matters.
limitations: conceptual/taxonomic, not a quantitative meta-analysis with pooled effect sizes
not specific to financial products
abstract-only, no numeric estimates
packets.relevance_reason: General consumer-behavior review addressing exactly the downstream persistence and heterogeneity questions the brief poses, without the employer-pension framing.
packets.title: How default choice architecture impacts downstream behavior: A taxonomy, theoretical framework, and research agenda
packets.abstract: Much is known about the immediate effects of default choice architecture and their underlying psychological processes. Yet, significant gaps remain in understanding if, when, and how defaults produce downstream effects on consumer behavior. We resolve conceptual ambiguity around downstream default effects by developing a taxonomy to categorize them and proposing a conceptual framework that illuminates the dynamic interplay of consumers' thoughts and actions with choice architecture as they engage in decision making over time. Applying this framework, we synthesize the current state of knowledge about downstream default effects, producing insights into multiple intersecting factors that modulate them. These include the time course of choice and consumption, consumers' antecedent preferences, and the salience of trade‐offs within and across choices. This theorizing guides our compilation of a research agenda for reconciling inconsistent prior findings and advancing understanding of how defaults interact with individual differences and contextual factors to influence later behavior.

packets.key_finding: Pre-checked recurring-donation defaults on political campaign websites increased donations by over $43 million while also increasing refund requests by almost $3 million, with the largest impact on smaller, less-experienced donors who did not compensate by changing donation amounts.
packets.methodology: Staggered difference-in-differences design exploiting different rollout timing of pre-checked recurring-donation defaults across 2020 U.S. campaign websites.
packets.why_it_matters: Directly demonstrates the mechanism the brief's support team worries about: a default creating an unintended recurring commitment lifts nominal sign-up but generates disproportionate refunds/complaints among smaller, less experienced users, the clearest quantified analogue to round-up opt-out risk.
limitations: Political donations, not a savings product
No 6-12 month engagement or withdrawal outcomes reported
packets.relevance_reason: Best-quantified real-world evidence of a recurring-commitment default producing both enrolment gains and manipulation-like backlash, closely analogous to the round-up opt-out risk.
packets.title: Dark defaults: How choice architecture steers political campaign donations
packets.abstract: In the months before the 2020 U.S. election, several political campaign websites added prechecked boxes (defaults), automatically making all donations into recurring weekly contributions unless donors unchecked them. Since these changes occurred at different times for different campaigns, we use a staggered difference-in-differences design to measure the causal effects of defaults on donors' behavior. We estimate that defaults increased campaign donations by over $43 million while increasing requested refunds by almost $3 million. The weekly default only impacted weekly recurring donations, and not other donations, suggesting that donors may not have intended to make weekly donations. The longer defaults were displayed, the more money campaigns raised through weekly donations. Donors did not compensate by changing the amount they donated. We found that the default had a larger impact on smaller donors and on donors who had no prior experience with defaults, causing them to start more chains and donate a larger proportion of their money through weekly recurring donations.
packets.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

packets.key_finding: A structural model of 8.6 million NYC taxi tipping decisions finds default adherence arises from the interaction of a deviation cost and an opt-out cost (84% of adherence needs both), and a counterfactual adding a 15% tip option below the existing 20/25/30% menu would capture 69% of the achievable consumer welfare gain at a 5.4% revenue cost.
packets.methodology: Structural econometric model estimated on large-scale transaction data plus an independent stated-preference survey to identify true preferences.
packets.why_it_matters: The closest available quantitative precedent for the preset-multiplier decision: it shows how a menu of preset options (analogous to 1x/2x/5x) anchors choice through friction rather than reshaping preference, and quantifies the welfare cost/benefit of adding or changing menu options \u2014 directly informing what levels to preset and whether an empty field would perform differently.
limitations: tipping decisions, not savings contributions
consumer payment app setting, not a savings product specifically
no persistence or long-run engagement outcomes
packets.relevance_reason: Directly analogous structural evidence on how preset menu options anchor consumer choice, in a self-directed digital consumer payment setting.
packets.title: Defaults and Decisions: Choice Architecture and Consumer Opt-Out
packets.abstract:
Why do consumers accept defaults (preset or suggested options)? This paper estimates a structural model that disentangles two frictions underlying default adherence: a deviation cost (the disutility when the final choice differs from the consumer’s ideal) and an opt-out cost (the effort to override the default). I estimate the model on 8.6 million tipping decisions from NYC Yellow taxi trips. A stated-preference survey identifies consumer tipping preferences independently of defaults. The central finding is friction complementarity: 84% of default adherence arises from the interaction of both frictions; remove either friction and the remaining one alone cannot sustain default adherence. Structural parameters are approximately stable when default options change, consistent with defaults channeling behavior through choice frictions rather than reshaping preferences. Counterfactual analysis shows that adding a 15% tip option below the existing 20%–25%–30% menu captures 69% of the achievable consumer welfare gain at a 5.4% revenue cost.
 This paper was accepted by Dube, Jean-Pierre, marketing.
 Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.05272 .

packets.key_finding: In a 220-participant RCT on voluntary pension saving decisions in China, behavioural nudges including default options significantly reduced willingness to contribute and the share of income allocated to saving, contrary to prevailing international evidence, with the largest backfire effects for positive-narrative and default-option nudges.
packets.methodology: Randomized controlled trial via online survey testing social-norm, framing, default-option, and narrative nudges on voluntary pension contribution decisions (n=220).
packets.why_it_matters: Directly contradicts the brief's working assumption that defaults reliably lift enrolment, the most explicit counter-evidence in the shortlist that a default can backfire and reduce contribution, with heterogeneity by income, education, and gender.
limitations: Hypothetical online-survey decisions rather than a live product
Small sample (n=220) and a non-EU, non-fintech cultural context (China)
packets.relevance_reason: The clearest contradicting evidence in the set, directly answering the brief's request for a paper contesting the 'defaults always help' premise.
packets.title: When Nudges Backfire: The Effect of Social Norms, Framing Effects, and Default Options on the Pension Saving Decisions in China
packets.abstract: This study investigates the impact of behavioral nudgessocial norms, loss aversion framing, default options, and positive narrativeon voluntary pension saving decisions in China. Using a randomized controlled trial administered via an online survey with 220 participants, we examine how these interventions influence both the willingness to contribute and the proportion of income allocated to pension savings. Contrary to prevailing international evidence, our results indicate that all nudges significantly reduce willingness to contribute relative to a control group, with the most substantial backfire effects observed for positive narrative and default option nudges. Furthermore, we identify important heterogeneity effects across income groups and emphasize the moderating roles of education, gender, and financial motivation. These findings underscore the critical importance of cultural, institutional, and individual factors in the design and implementation of behavioral interventions. Policy measures tailored to specific demographic segments and focused on financial education and trust-building are recommended.
packets.venue: Advances in Economics, Management and Political Sciences

packets.key_finding: This chapter synthesizes household-finance research on consumption/saving, choice architecture, and product-design interventions (education, defaults, advice, disclosure) that shape financial behavior.
packets.methodology: Narrative literature review/book chapter summarizing empirical regularities and behavioral interventions in household finance.
packets.why_it_matters: Provides the broader map of choice-architecture tools beyond defaults and situates default effects among alternatives like disclosure or advice, supplying the synthesis-level context the brief asked for beyond a single study.
limitations: narrative overview, not a systematic review or meta-analysis with pooled effect sizes
covers mostly employer retirement and general household finance rather than a fintech round-up product specifically
no quantitative effect sizes in the abstract
packets.relevance_reason: The broad review/synthesis of behavioral household-finance interventions the brief calls for, situating default and choice-architecture effects in context.
packets.title: Behavioral Household Finance
packets.abstract: This chapter provides an overview of household finance. The first part summarizes key facts regarding household financial behavior, emphasizing empirical regularities that are inconsistent with the standard classical economic model and discussing extensions of the classical model and explanations grounded in behavioral economics that can account for the observed patterns. This part covers five topics: consumption and savings, borrowing, payments, asset allocation, and insurance. The second part addresses interventions that firms, governments, and other parties deploy to shape household financial outcomes: education and information, peer effects and social influence, product design, advice and disclosure, choice architecture, and interventions that directly target prices or quantities.

packets.key_finding: A field experiment with payment reminders reduced credit card late fees by 14% but increased overdraft fees by 9%, with users who had a history of overdraft use experiencing a net 5% increase in total fees while everyone else saved 15%.
packets.methodology: Randomized field experiment with a financial management platform in Brazil; fee outcomes tracked across credit card and checking accounts.
packets.why_it_matters: Gives quantified evidence that a well-intentioned nudge can help most users while making a specific, identifiable subgroup worse off — directly bears on the brief's requirement not to ship a default that looks good on average while harming vulnerable users, and argues for monitoring heterogeneous effects (e.g. by liquidity/overdraft history) rather than a single enrolment metric.
limitations: studies payment reminders, not enrolment defaults or preset contribution levels
credit card/overdraft fee context rather than round-up savings
no data on persistence beyond the fee-measurement period
packets.relevance_reason: Best available quantified evidence in this batch for the brief's explicit concern about who is helped versus hurt by a nudge in a consumer financial product.
packets.title: Side Effects of Nudging: Evidence from a Randomized Intervention in the Credit Card Market
packets.abstract: Abstract This paper studies the direct and indirect effects of nudging, by means of a field experiment with a financial management platform in Brazil. Reminders for upcoming credit card payments reduced credit card late-payment fees by 14%, but increased overdraft fees in checking accounts by 9%. The unintended effect is concentrated in users with a history of overdraft use. These users experienced a net increase of 5% in total fees, while the rest experienced savings of 15%. The results provide clear insights for nudge design: like any policy action, nudges can have side effects, and one size may not fit all.

alternates.key_finding: People generally approve of financial nudges/interventions, with strongest approval for those framed around savings and targeting deliberate (System 2) rather than automatic (System 1) processing; younger, female, urban, higher-income respondents favor them most.
alternates.methodology: Pre-registered survey experiment; 2,100 representative Australian respondents rated 36 hypothetical financial intervention scenarios varying transparency, framing (spending vs. saving), and System (1 vs. 2) on approval, ethics, manipulation, and likelihood of use.
alternates.why_it_matters: Suggests our round-up feature should be framed in savings terms and lean toward deliberate/System-2 mechanisms (favoring active choice over covert opt-out) to be seen as helpful rather than manipulative — directly informs the messaging and framing around whichever entry design we choose.
limitations: hypothetical vignette approval, not actual enrollment or savings behavior
Australian sample rather than EU regulatory context
self-reported approval may not predict real complaint or withdrawal behavior
alternates.relevance_reason: Directly tests when a financial default/nudge is perceived as manipulative vs. beneficial, the exact reputational-risk question the brief raises.
alternates.title: Do people like financial nudges?
alternates.abstract: Abstract Do people like financial nudges? To answer that question we conducted a pre-registered survey presenting people with 36 hypothetical scenarios describing financial interventions. We varied levels of transparency (i.e., explaining how the interventions worked), framing (interventions framed in terms of spending, or saving), and ‘System’ (interventions could target either System 1 or System 2). Participants were a random sample of 2,100 people drawn from a representative Australian population. All financial interventions were tested across six dependent variables: approval, benefit, ethics, manipulation, the likelihood of use, as well as the likelihood of use if the intervention were to be proposed by a bank. Results indicate that people generally approve of financial interventions, rating them as neutral to positive across all dependent variables (except for manipulation, which was reverse coded). We find effects of framing and System. People have strong and significant preferences for System 2 interventions, and interventions framed in terms of savings. Transparency was not found to have a significant impact on how people rate financial interventions. Financial interventions continue to be rated positive, regardless of the messenger. Looking at demographics, we find that participants who were female, younger, living in metro areas and earning higher incomes were most likely to favor financial interventions, and this effect is especially strong for those aged under 45. We discuss the implications for these results as applied to the financial sector.

alternates.key_finding: Large-scale UK bank field experiments show automatic enrollment into just-in-time overdraft text alerts cuts unarranged overdraft charges 17-19% and arranged overdraft charges 4-8%, implying £170-240 million in annual market-wide savings, though alerts only capture less than half of consumers' potential savings.
alternates.methodology: At-scale randomized field experiments run at major UK banks.
alternates.why_it_matters: Shows that automatic enrollment into a real consumer-banking-app feature produces quantified, real behaviour change rather than only nominal sign-up, the closest available evidence bearing on whether opt-out enrolment into round-ups would move actual financial behaviour.
limitations: Overdraft alerts, not a savings/round-up product
No 6-12 month persistence data reported in the abstract
alternates.relevance_reason: Closest real consumer-banking-app auto-enrollment field experiment with quantified effect sizes, directly analogous to the round-up feature's opt-out design.
alternates.title: Sending Out an SMS: Automatic Enrollment Experiments for Overdraft Alerts
alternates.abstract: ABSTRACT At‐scale field experiments at major U.K. banks show that automatic enrollment into “just‐in‐time” text alerts reduces unarranged overdraft and unpaid item charges 17% to 19% and arranged overdraft charges 4% to 8%, implying annual market‐wide savings of £170 million to £240 million. Incremental benefits from “early‐warning” alerts are statistically insignificant, although economically significant effects are not ruled out. Prior to the experiments, over half of overdrafts could have been avoided by using lower‐cost liquidity available in savings and credit card accounts. Alerts help consumers achieve less than half of these potential savings.

alternates.key_finding: Field experiments show that requiring an explicit choice ('active choice'), and especially an 'enhanced active choice' that highlights the losses of not choosing the preferred option, can motivate behavior change as an alternative or complement to automatic-enrollment defaults.
alternates.methodology: Review of prior default/active-choice literature plus two field experiments testing active choice and enhanced active choice interventions.
alternates.why_it_matters: Introduces and validates the active-choice design that is one of the brief's two open decisions, plus a specific 'enhanced' variant (highlighting the cost of opting out) we could adapt for our forced-choice onboarding screen to capture more enrollment benefit without full passive opt-out.
limitations: primarily tested in medication-adherence/health contexts; financial savings application discussed but not directly field-tested here
abstract gives no numeric effect sizes
2011 paper, predates current app/regulatory context
alternates.relevance_reason: Directly introduces and tests the active-choice and enhanced-active-choice designs central to the brief's first open decision.
alternates.title: Enhanced active choice: A new method to motivate behavior change
alternates.abstract: Abstract High rates of medication non‐adherence have significant public health and economic consequences. In other contexts such as savings behavior, opt‐out policies, in which the alternative preferred by the policy maker is made the default, have gotten great traction but may not be feasible in health care settings. After reviewing previous applications, we present a series of studies, including two field experiments, that test the effectiveness of an alternative, ‘active choice’ policy in which there is no default, but decision makers are required to make a choice (Carroll, Choi, Laibson, Madrian, & Metrick, 2009; Spital, 1993, 1995). In addition, we propose and test a modified version of active choice, that we call ‘enhanced active choice’ that favors one alternative by highlighting losses incumbent in the in the non‐preferred alternative. We recommend Enhanced Active Choice as a complement to automatic enrollment or when automatic enrollment is infeasible or unethical.

alternates.key_finding: An opt-in short-term (anytime-withdrawal) payroll savings program at five UK firms saw excellent retention among adopters \u2014 96% still held a balance and 87% still received an automatic contribution after 12 months \u2014 but take-up was extremely low, with at most 0.7% of eligible employees ever activating an account.
alternates.methodology: Field study of the rollout of an opt-in liquid, anytime-withdrawal savings account program across five UK employers.
alternates.why_it_matters: This is the closest product-structure match to the round-up feature (liquid, withdraw-anytime savings, not retirement) and shows opt-in alone can produce vanishingly small enrollment despite the product working well for those who adopt it \u2014 direct evidence against relying on opt-in for the entry decision.
limitations: delivered via employer payroll, not a standalone consumer app
no comparison to opt-out or active-choice enrollment in this study
UK employer sample, not EU consumer banking app users
alternates.relevance_reason: Uniquely close product analog (liquid, anytime-withdrawal savings) showing opt-in enrollment failure despite strong retention among adopters.
alternates.title: Employer-Based Short-Term Savings Accounts
alternates.abstract: We study the introduction of a choice architecture design intended to increase short-term savings among employees at five U.K. firms. Employees were offered the opportunity to opt into a payroll deduction program that auto-deposits funds from each paycheck into a short-term savings account from which withdrawals are possible at any time. We find that employees who opted into the program kept using it. Among employees whose accounts were created early enough to be observed over the first 12 months after their account activation and who did not separate from employment during this period, 96% still had a balance greater than 1 and 87% received an automatic payroll contribution in month 12. However, product take-up was very low: no more than 0.7% of eligible employees ever activated an account. Opt-in access to short-term savings programs does not elicit widespread participation.

alternates.key_finding: EU law regulates dark patterns as violations of consumer autonomy, and the article develops a six-category taxonomy of autonomy violations (including pre-selected defaults) to distinguish acceptable choice-architecture influence from regulable manipulation.
alternates.methodology: Legal/normative analysis mapping EU dark-pattern law and constructing an autonomy-violation taxonomy. abstract-only.
alternates.why_it_matters: Gives the specific EU legal framework for judging whether an opt-out entry design would read as a regulable dark pattern versus a helpful default, directly addressing the brief's EU reputational-risk constraint.
limitations: Legal/normative analysis, not empirical evidence on enrolment or savings behaviour
No effect sizes or behavioural outcomes
alternates.relevance_reason: Supplies the EU dark-pattern/autonomy framework the brief explicitly asks for when weighing opt-out against active choice.
alternates.title: Regulating Dark Patterns
alternates.abstract: Dark patterns have become increasingly pervasive in online choice architectures, encompassing practices like subscription traps, hiding information about fees, pre-selecting options by default, nagging, and drip pricing. Regulators around the world have started to express concerns that such practices are causing substantial consumer detriment. This Article focuses on the legal response to dark patterns in the European Union. It provides the first comprehensive mapping of European Union laws expressly addressing dark patterns. The Article argues that these laws protect biased consumers and adopt autonomy as a normative lens to assess dark patterns. Consequently, regulating dark patterns in European Union law means regulating for autonomy. This normative lens is under-researched. This Article addresses this gap in research with two principle contributions. First, it works out a specific conception of autonomous decision-making, rooted in the paradigm that providing consumers with information enables consumers to make an informed decision. Second, the Article offers a novel normative classification for dark patterns in online choice architectures. It develops a taxonomy encompassing six categories of autonomy violations, specifically tailored for the assessment and regulation of dark patterns that exploit consumer behavioral biases. These categories serve multiple purposes. They uncover and make explicit the autonomy violations addressed by existing European Union laws. They delineate the contentious line between acceptable influences on consumer decision-making and autonomy violations that may warrant regulation in online choice architectures. They also provide policymakers in the EU and elsewhere with a framework when deliberating the regulation of other instances of dark patterns.
